title: I’m building a game designed to keep growing after I’m gone
author: WolrdInDust
selftext:
https://reddit.com/link/1tyw1af/video/1x63zqerxq5h1/player

Most games stop growing when the creator stops adding content.

I’m trying to build something different: a browser game that can keep expanding through the players who beat it.

The game is called **WorldClaimed Chain**.

The core loop is:

**play → clear → claim → describe → generate → validate → extend**

A player clears the active Chain, reaches a Reward Gate, and earns a World Slot. Then they describe the next world in plain language, and the system turns that idea into a playable stage.

I’m calling the model **IdeaChain**:

**completion becomes creation.**

The player does not need to be a level designer. They do not open a level editor. They just beat the run and describe the world they want to add.

The AI/game-dev challenge is making that safe.

I do **not** want:

**prompt → arbitrary code → live level**

That would become chaos very quickly.

The pipeline I’m aiming for is:

**player idea → structured blueprint → controlled game components → validation → playable stage**

So the AI helps turn imagination into a stage, but the game engine stays the source of truth.

The long-term vision is a living chain of playable worlds: each accepted stage becomes part of the Chain Ledger, with attribution to the player who created it.

Playable soft launch:  
[https://worldclaimed.com/chain](https://worldclaimed.com/chain)

I’d love feedback from AI game devs:

1. Would you use JSON blueprints as the source of truth?
2. How would you validate AI-generated levels before publishing them?
3. Would you use automated playtesting, deterministic simulation, replay validation, or human review?
4. Does the “beat the game → describe the next world → AI makes it playable” loop feel strong enough as a player motivation?

This is an independent experiment, not affiliated with OpenAI. I’m sharing it because I think AI-generated game content needs strong constraints, not just bigger prompts.

comments.author: Felfedezni
comments.body: Great idea but ugh why another flappy bird clone?

replies.author: WolrdInDust
replies.body:
Fair question 😄

I picked a Flappy Bird-like loop mostly because it’s instantly understandable. Everyone knows the basic skill test, so I could focus on the actual experiment: **what happens after you beat it.**

The important part for me isn’t the clone itself. It could be Flappy Bird, Icy Tower, an endless runner, or something else. The core idea is that when someone clears the game, they can add a new piece of the world and leave a permanent trace behind.

So even if I stop working on it one day, the chain can keep growing as long as players keep beating it and adding their own worlds.

replies.author: WolrdInDust
replies.body:
To clarify the bigger idea: I don’t see IdeaChain only as a platform, but more as a model for how games or apps can evolve.

The key concept is that a player who completes the challenge earns the right to leave a permanent trace inside the experience. Not just a name on a leaderboard, but something that actually pushes the world forward: a new stage, rule, mechanic, character, story piece, or gameplay element.

So the game is not only created by the original developer. It keeps growing through the people who beat it.

comments.author: whathappenedtomycake
comments.body: I mean from the video the “new” level just looks like a different static background image.

replies.author: WolrdInDust
replies.body:
Fair criticism. The current video shows mostly the visual layer, so it can look like just a static background swap.

The bigger idea is that winning a run gives the player the ability to add a new piece of the world — not only a background, but eventually layout, rules, enemies/NPCs, obstacles, objectives and mechanics.

Right now it’s an early slice of the IdeaChain loop: **complete → claim → describe → generate → play.**  
The video doesn’t fully sell that yet, but that’s exactly the direction.

comments.author: Itchy-Individual3536
comments.body:
It's an interesting idea for sure. The biggest challenge I think is finding the sweet spot between very constraint but safe changes and complete openness to players' ideas. Too many constraints and the new levels are repetitive and boring, too few and there will either be unplayable levels or ones that are way too easy, or you'll get NSFW stuff in there pretty soon. Or players would rig the game so that they can keep adding level after level. Human malevolence may never be underestimated, even if it's just done for the heck of it.

I also think flappy bird is a boring example to apply this mechanic to, but I understand you take this just as a proof of concept for now. It's interesting to think about how this concept could be applied to different genres differently.

replies.author: WolrdInDust
replies.body:
Thanks, this is exactly the kind of feedback I was hoping for.

I agree that the hardest part is not the idea itself, but the boundary between freedom and control. If the system is too constrained, player-created stages become repetitive. If it is too open, you quickly get impossible levels, trivial levels, exploits, spam, or content that should never be in the game.

The way I’m thinking about IdeaChain is not:

player prompt → arbitrary level goes live

but rather:

player earns a World Slot → describes the idea → the system converts it into a structured blueprint → the model/game validates it → unsafe, unplayable, NSFW, copyrighted, or abusive content is rejected → only accepted stages can enter the Chain.

So the reward is creative authorship, but inside a validated framework.

And yes, I agree about the current Flappy-like prototype. It is mainly a proof of concept for the IdeaChain loop: beat the game, claim the next world, describe it, and let the system turn it into a playable stage.

I’m already working on a new game using the same IdeaChain Model, with a more original one-tap mechanic. The goal is to prove that the model can work beyond this first prototype and that “completion becomes creation” can be applied to different genres.

Really appreciate the thoughtful comment.

comments.author: Cute_Ad8981
comments.body: There was someone who posted a game (i think it was some kind of 2d shooter game) where people could prompt for levels. i think many ai games use that kind of mechanic, where players can prompt for in-game designs. maybe you can look them up and find ideas.

replies.author: WolrdInDust
replies.body: Thank you, others on epwno think similarly. I just want to create a framework where the winner can describe the next level and be the first to play it, and they will always be part of the game. I was going through a difficult period in my life and decided I wanted to create something good that would give me the feeling of being part of something bigger.

comments.author: WolrdInDust
comments.body: Thank you for all the comments. I think the idea chain concept is correct, and I could have used an original game as an example. I thought it would be easier to present it on something familiar. Soon, I'll present my original game on this framework, and whoever wins will be able to expand the game to a new level!
